title: Affordable Housing
if_approved: The city could borrow up to $22 million for its Affordable Housing Program, such as buying and fixing up run-down property, building or renovating homes, and helping people rent or buy. Which projects get the money, and when, would be decided later.
arguments_for: City planners describe the loan as money set aside exclusively for affordable housing. According to the [city's capital improvement program](https://www.baltimorecity.gov/planning/our-work/capital-improvement-program/go-bonds), eligible uses include buying and preserving property, producing new housing, demolition, rental assistance, housing counseling, and loans or grants for projects, and the money could support the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. The loan is authorized for up to \$22 million over two years.
arguments_against: Critics of the bond package say voters are being asked to approve borrowing without enough detail. [David Williams](https://www.kansascity.com/news/nation-world/national/article317884063.html), president of the Taxpayers Protection Alliance, told the Baltimore Sun the question is “just some wording on a ballot” with “no explanation” of why the city chose that amount, and that bonds cost taxpayers more in the long run because of interest. The same report noted that the ballot questions describe what the money may be used for rather than committing it to specific projects.
keywords: affordable housing; housing bond; rent help; home buying help; city borrowing

title: School Facilities
if_approved: The city could borrow up to $60 million for public school buildings, equipment, and athletic facilities, including some that also serve community health and recreation. Which schools get the money would be decided later.
arguments_for: City planners say the loan complements the nearly billion-dollar 21st Century Schools initiative by paying for systemwide needs it does not cover, such as fire alarms and HVAC systems, according to the [city's capital improvement program](https://www.baltimorecity.gov/planning/our-work/capital-improvement-program/go-bonds). It would also let the city match state funding through the Public School Construction Program for improvements outside that initiative, and it allows additional schools to be renovated or replaced. The loan is authorized for up to \$60 million over two years.
arguments_against: Critics say the city has not shown what the school money would buy. [David Williams](https://www.kansascity.com/news/nation-world/national/article317884063.html) of the Taxpayers Protection Alliance told the Baltimore Sun the city could have said how many schools need to be refurbished and what that would cost, and that “we don't see any of that detail.” The report noted the ballot questions list permitted uses rather than committing specific amounts to individual schools. It also noted that Moody's lowered the city's credit rating in August, which could make future borrowing more expensive, though the downgrade did not establish that Baltimore cannot afford the borrowing.
keywords: schools; school buildings; school bond; school repairs; athletic fields; city borrowing

title: Community And Economic Development
if_approved: The city could borrow up to $50 million for neighborhood and economic development, such as cleaning up blighted property, improving neighborhoods, helping people with housing, and supporting businesses. The money could be used for loans and grants as well as direct projects. Which ones get funded would be decided later.
arguments_for: City planners say community and economic development takes investment in neighborhoods, not just housing and jobs, so the money could also pay for public infrastructure that supports those goals, such as parks, recreation centers, transportation infrastructure, libraries, and health centers, according to the [city's capital improvement program](https://www.baltimorecity.gov/planning/our-work/capital-improvement-program/go-bonds). The loan is authorized for up to \$50 million over two years.
arguments_against: Critics point to the growing pace of borrowing. [The Baltimore Sun reported](https://www.kansascity.com/news/nation-world/national/article317884063.html) that residents authorized \$160 million in bonds in 2022 and \$250 million in 2024, and that this year's \$280 million across four questions is a 75% increase from four years ago. University of Maryland finance professor Cliff Rossi said the borrowing would add roughly 9% to the city's existing debt, calling it “a new debt burden for a city that is already stressed fiscally.”
keywords: blighted property; neighborhood improvement; business grants; economic development; city borrowing

title: Public Infrastructure
if_approved: The city could borrow up to $148 million for public infrastructure: city buildings, libraries, parks, streets, utilities, technology, and similar improvements. Which projects get the money would be decided later.
arguments_for: City officials say the need is growing while a major funding source shrinks. [The Baltimore Sun reported](https://www.kansascity.com/news/nation-world/national/article317884063.html) that state Highway User Revenue is scheduled to fall beginning in fiscal 2028, and that under projections capital transportation funding could drop from about \$91 million in fiscal 2027 to about \$24.7 million in fiscal 2028, a cut of more than 70%. City officials have warned this could force reductions in road resurfacing, alley repairs, bridge work, and traffic signal replacements. The [city's capital improvement program](https://www.baltimorecity.gov/planning/our-work/capital-improvement-program/go-bonds) lists eligible uses including parks, recreation centers, libraries, streets, bridges, sidewalks, and public safety buildings.
arguments_against: Critics question whether borrowing is the right way to pay for maintenance. University of Maryland finance professor Cliff Rossi told [the Baltimore Sun](https://www.kansascity.com/news/nation-world/national/article317884063.html) that much of the infrastructure money would go to repair and rehabilitate existing assets rather than build new ones, so “you take on 20 years of interest on building maintenance and road maintenance that might only last 5 to 10 years.” He asked whether that is worth it. David Williams of the Taxpayers Protection Alliance said taxpayers should be careful because bonds can end up costing them much more in interest.
keywords: infrastructure; streets; libraries; parks; city buildings; technology; city borrowing

title: Contract Bidding And Awards
if_approved: The charter's rules that contracts go to the lowest bidder, how to break ties, and which bonds contractors must provide would be removed on November 7, 2028, unless the city passes its own rules on the topic sooner. The city could then change how it awards contracts through city laws or regulations, without going back to voters.
arguments_for: Supporters argue the lowest-bid rule rewards contractors who bid low and then raise the price through change orders. [Councilman Ryan Dorsey](https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/local-government/baltimore-contracts-city-council-ballot-question-4PSCT4XUZFBMRP73UWKT573O4E/), who led the Council committee that drafted the charter amendments, cited the Harford Road Bridge, where a Virginia-based contractor needed 17 change orders and pushed the project millions over budget. Without the charter rule, he said, the city could score bids on factors such as local hiring or a contractor's past performance. Council President Zeke Cohen said the change lets the Board of Estimates “determine which contract best serves the public interest,” and Mayor Brandon Scott argued a local vendor bidding \$425,000 can be a better value than an out-of-state bid of \$400,000 because the money stays in Baltimore.
arguments_against: Reporting on the measure points to favoritism as the main risk. [The Baltimore Banner reported](https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/local-government/baltimore-contracts-city-council-ballot-question-4PSCT4XUZFBMRP73UWKT573O4E/) that bringing factors other than cost into bidding creates the possibility of favoritism, and that costs could also increase, although Scott argued the final price may be lower. The amendment does not write the new bidding rules; it leaves them to city officials, who must still decide how bids will be scored. Dorsey said the city will have to approach that “thoughtfully” and build in guardrails, and Cohen said he and the Council are committed to developing them.
keywords: contracts; lowest bidder; city contracting; bidding rules; charter change

title: Budget Process And Board Of Estimates
if_approved: The mayor, not the Board of Estimates, would prepare the city budget, and the Board would lose many of its other duties, which could be handed to other city offices. The time to veto a bill and override a veto would be shortened, the preliminary budget hearings would end, and the $1 million limit on the emergency fund would be removed. Most changes start December 3, 2026. Removed charter sections go away on November 7, 2028, unless the city replaces them sooner. The new veto and approval rules start December 5, 2028.
arguments_for: Supporters say the budget process is outdated and the Board of Estimates is lopsided. [Comptroller Bill Henry](https://www.baltimorecity.gov/comptroller/news/comptroller-henry-question-f-and-the-future-of-baltimore-city-government), who did not endorse the measure, noted the current charter makes the Board wait 30 days on a draft budget the mayor effectively submitted to themself, and said moving the budget to the Council sooner gives it time to gather public input and negotiate with the mayor, which matters more now that the state requires the tax rate to be certified sooner. Council President Zeke Cohen told [WBAL-TV](https://www.wbaltv.com/article/baltimore-question-f-board-of-estimates-city-spending-power/73595723) the change gives the Council more time to negotiate the budget, called the current system antiquated, and noted the mayor controls three votes on the Board. Mayor Brandon Scott has said he supports the question and that the Board's responsibilities should be governed by city code.
arguments_against: Critics worry it moves power without a plan. [Comptroller Bill Henry](https://www.baltimorecity.gov/comptroller/news/comptroller-henry-question-f-and-the-future-of-baltimore-city-government) said a yes vote “requires a leap of faith” that the mayor and Council will protect transparency, because the amendment lets the Council reassign many Board duties, such as approving emergency contracts and collective bargaining agreements, by ordinance, and there is no clear public plan for who would do what. He called it a possible precursor to a 2028 amendment to eliminate the Board, which he said could help or hurt oversight depending on whether decisions end up behind closed doors. [WBAL-TV](https://www.wbaltv.com/article/baltimore-question-f-board-of-estimates-city-spending-power/73595723) reported the measure would shift approval of property tax rates, revenue estimates, and employee salaries to the mayor or departments under his control in late 2028, though Cohen said that is not the plan.
keywords: city budget; Board of Estimates; mayor budget power; veto; emergency fund; charter change

title: Franchises And Minor Privileges
if_approved: The stormwater system could never be sold or rented out. Space in the conduit system could be rented out, but the system itself still couldn't be sold. Minor privileges (small permissions to use part of city property) would be granted by a city agency under a process set by city law, instead of by the Board of Estimates, and outdated language about street railways and trackless trolleys would be removed. Most changes start December 3, 2026. Removed charter sections go away on November 7, 2028, unless the city replaces them sooner.
arguments_for: Supporters say routing small, routine approvals such as sidewalk signage through an agency process, rather than the Board of Estimates, could speed up approvals for residents and small businesses, according to the [VOTE411 voter guide](https://onyourballot.vote411.org/m/race-detail.do?id=4403211), which credits Baltimore Votes for the arguments. The amendment would also add the stormwater system to the list of city property that can never be sold or rented out as a franchise.
arguments_against: Some voters may prefer keeping these approvals with an elected board, since the Board of Estimates currently offers more direct public accountability than an internal agency process, according to the same [VOTE411 voter guide](https://onyourballot.vote411.org/m/race-detail.do?id=4403211). I did not find named opponents or organized opposition to this question.
keywords: minor privileges; franchises; stormwater; conduit; city property; Board of Estimates; charter change

title: Department Of Water And Wastewater
if_approved: A new city Department of Water and Wastewater, with its own director, would take over the water supply and wastewater systems from the Department of Public Works on January 1, 2029. The charter requirement that bureaus within Public Works be created or eliminated by city law would also be removed.
arguments_for: [The Baltimore Banner reported](https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/local-government/baltimore-ballot-questions-baby-bonus-IBGEZCUQHBBD5IWQ3MYZNOVWKU/) that the amendment separates the water and wastewater utilities from the Department of Public Works in an effort to improve the city's bond rating for water and wastewater. It also better positions the city to regionalize direction of the water and sewer systems, which serve Baltimore County and other jurisdictions as well.
keywords: water; wastewater; water department; sewer; public works; charter change

title: Baltimore Baby Fund
if_approved: The Baltimore Baby Fund would be created as a separate city fund, starting December 3, 2026. Beginning in fiscal year 2028, the city would add 3 cents for every $100 of taxable property value each year. Estimates of the yearly amount range from about $15 million (the Maryland Child Alliance, as reported by WYPR) to $17 million (as reported by FOX45). The fund could also accept donations and grants. The money could only be used for families with newborns, and it couldn't replace newborn funding already in the budget.
arguments_for: Supporters argue the fund would be an investment in Baltimore's future and in families with newborns, without raising property taxes. [Nate Golden](https://www.wypr.org/wypr-news/2026-10-15/baltimore-ballot-question-could-set-aside-millions-for-babies), president of the Maryland Child Alliance and a high school math teacher, told WYPR that many problems in schools are really economic problems, that the measure would not raise property taxes, and that tying the fund to taxable property value helps it keep pace with inflation. Mayor Brandon Scott, who [urged residents to vote yes](https://foxbaltimore.com/news/local/baltimore-voters-baby-bonus-program-cost-oversigt), told FOX45 that direct cash payments to families of infants have been tied to better test scores, higher future income for parents and young people, fewer child protective services referrals, and less time in foster care. FOX45 noted the proposal follows a pilot that gave 200 families \$1,000 a month after the birth of a child.
arguments_against: Critics question whether voters have enough information to decide. [Taxpayer advocate David Williams](https://foxbaltimore.com/news/local/baltimore-voters-baby-bonus-program-cost-oversigt) told FOX45 the fund “is not ready to be voted on” because of unanswered questions about how big the program will be, and he raised concerns about oversight. FOX45 reported that the mayor's executive order outlines one-time payments plus monthly help for qualifying low-income families, but exact amounts and eligibility are not final. Williams also questioned whether the city can afford another long-term commitment tied to property taxes, saying it makes property tax cuts harder. [WYPR](https://www.wypr.org/wypr-news/2026-10-15/baltimore-ballot-question-could-set-aside-millions-for-babies) reported further opposition from people who say families should not have children they cannot afford; organizers respond by pointing to the needs of children already born.
keywords: baby bonus; baby fund; newborn; cash for parents; families with newborns; citizen petition

title: Baltimore City Police Department
if_approved: The Police Department would be written into the city charter as a city agency headed by a Police Commissioner, whom the mayor would appoint, subject to confirmation. The commissioner would decide how the department is organized and run. The charter would also spell out the department's job (keeping the peace, preventing and investigating crime, enforcing laws, and making arrests) and set the process for creating police districts.

title: Inner Harbor Park
if_approved: A charter rule that dedicates the Inner Harbor shoreline to public park use would change. Up to 4.5 acres (up from 3.2) near Conway Street could be used for restaurants, businesses, multifamily housing, and parking, and areas used for housing and parking would no longer count as part of the public park. Approval alone wouldn't mean anything gets built.
keywords: Inner Harbor; waterfront park; Conway Street; restaurants and housing; park land; charter change

title: Community Reinvestment And Reparations Fund
if_approved: A city fund would be created to pay for the work of the Community Reinvestment and Reparations Commission. Money in it would carry over from year to year instead of expiring, and it could only be used for the commission's work, within limits set by state law. The question doesn't set a dollar amount, and the City Council could pass laws on how the fund is overseen and run.
keywords: reparations; reinvestment fund; Community Reinvestment and Reparations Commission; charter change

title: Reducing The Size Of The City Council
if_approved: The City Council would shrink from 14 districts to 8. The mayor would have to draw a new district map based on the latest census and give it to the Council by February 1 of the first municipal election year afterward.
